newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian Air, unions hope for new survival deal.
newsitem.headline: Canadian Air, unions hope for new survival deal.

text.p: Canadian Airlines Corp. and four of its unions said Tuesday they were confident that a newly overhauled survival plan that includes various government financial breaks would be approved by Ottawa and two western provinces.
However, as the clock wound down to a midnight Wednesday deadline for all parties to reach a deal, two of Canadian's biggest unions had yet to sign onto the agreement.

Canadian has said it faces financial failure early next year unless the company, its unions, one-third owner AMR Corp., which is the parent of American Airlines, and federal and provincial governments approve a plan aimed at adding C$180 million ($135 million) a year to its bottom line.

Canadian Chief Executive Kevin Benson and leaders of the unions supporting the plan flew to Calgary, Alberta, from Vancouver, British Columbia, on Tuesday to present a strategy to Alberta Premier Ralph Klein that would see aviation fuel taxes cut in half and payments on a loan guaranteed by the province extended.

The governments of Canada and British Columbia were asked earlier in Vancouver to provide tax and loan breaks, with a total of C$35 million ($26 million) to be saved by the ailing carrier if they all agreed.

The government concessions would mean a previously hard-and-fast company call for 10-percent wage rollbacks for employees would be reduced to an average of 5 percent, with lower-income workers taking less of a cut and higher earners absorbing more.
Klein said after the meeting that the deal would be presented to the provincial cabinet and Alberta would agree to the measures if all the other parties signed on.
His government had announced lower fuel taxes to take effect for the 1998 fiscal year, but Canadian's plan would move the reduction up by 12 months.

"This airline is without doubt the backbone of air traffic in the West and really provides the only competition relative to the operation of commercial airline activity in Canada," Klein told reporters.
"And we're really interested in making sure that this airline survives -- its headquarters, of course, are here."
Alberta currently guarantees C$12 million ($9 million) of the remaining C$30 million ($23 million) in government-backed loans, with British Columbia and Canada making up the remainder.
"The response from the premier has put a smile on our face (but) the process has to continue," said Dave Ritchie of the International Association of Machinists.
Four of the company's unions have agreed to the new life-support strategy on the condition that requests for government involvement, which management initially rejected, be explored.
The plan includes the wage cuts among its 16,400 employees, major route restructurings and a C$48 million ($36 million) reduction in computer and management fees paid to Fort Worth-Tex.-based AMR.

Benson said he and the supporting unions now needed to convince the holdouts -- the Canadian Auto Workers and the Canadian Union of Public Employees -- that the reworked deal would protect employees at the lower end of the wage scale.
The CAW represents 3,700 workers at Canadian and the public employees union represents 2,700 workers.
"The quicker they can come on board and make this happen, the better," he said.

Benson said he was confident that AMR's portion of the plan would fall into place over the next two days if the CAW and the public employees union returned to the bargaining table and governments approve the new strategy.

In Vancouver, CAW negotiator Peggy Nash said late Tuesday that her union was sticking by its demands for a government bailout and re-regulation of Canada's domestic airline industry because of its view that employee wages were not the reason for Canadian's cash crunch.
Benson said the Nov. 27 deadline to reach a deal was necessary before approaching the carrier's creditors with a solid business plan at the end of this month.
